In 2007, Uzochukwu BS, Obikeze EN, Onwujekwe OE, Onoka CA, and Griffiths UK conducted a cost-effectiveness analysis comparing rapid diagnostic tests, microscopy, and syndromic approaches for malaria diagnosis in Nigeria. Their findings have implications for scaling up the deployment of artemisinin-based combination therapies (ACTs). (Malaria Journal, 2009; 8:265). 2. Batwala V, Magnussen P, Hansen KS, and Nuwaha F evaluated the cost-effectiveness of malaria microscopy and rapid diagnostic tests versus presumptive diagnosis in Uganda. Their study highlights the implications for malaria control strategies in the region. (Malaria Journal, 2011; 10:372). 3. Cohn J, Whitehouse K, Trang T, Tuttle J, and Lueck K systematically reviewed pediatric HIV testing beyond prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) programs, focusing on where to target testing efforts. (Web Supplement B). 4. McCollum ED, Johnson DC, Chasela CS, Siwande LD, Kazembe PN, Olson D, et al. compared early infant HIV diagnosis services at immunization clinics versus general pediatric clinics for children under five in Malawi. They found superior uptake and outcomes at immunization clinics. (Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, 2012; 60(4):e107–10). 5. Asafo-Agyei SB, Antwi S, and Nguah SB conducted a cross-sectional prospective study on HIV infection in severely malnourished children in Kumasi, Ghana. (BMC Pediatrics, 2013; 13:181). 6. Sweeney S, Obure CD, Maier CB, Greener R, Dehne K, and Vassall A systematically reviewed the costs and efficiency of integrating HIV/AIDS services with other health services. Their findings provide evidence and experience for improving service delivery. (Sexually Transmitted Infections, 2012; 88(2):85–99). 7. Ramirez-Avila L, Noubary F, Pansegrouw D, Sithole S, Giddy J, Losina E, et al. assessed the acceptability and feasibility of routine pediatric HIV testing in an outpatient clinic in Durban, South Africa. (Pediatric Infectious Disease Journal, 2013; 32(12):1348–53). 8. Kranzer K, Meghji J, Bandason T, Dauya E, Mungofa S, Busza J, et al. identified barriers to provider-initiated testing and counseling for children in high HIV prevalence settings through a mixed-methods study. (PLoS Medicine, 2014; 11(5):e1001649). 9. Ndiraungu J, Bärnighausen T, Tanser F, Tint K, and Newell ML examined childhood vaccination coverage and the impact of maternal HIV status on child vaccination in rural KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. (Tropical Medicine & International Health, 2009; 14(11):1383–93). 10. Goodson JL, Finkbeiner T, Davis NL, Lyimo D, Rwebembera A, Swartzendruber AL, et al. evaluated the use of routine infant immunization visits to identify and follow up on HIV-exposed infants and their mothers in Tanzania. (Journal of Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndromes, 2013; 63(1):e9–e15). 11. The UNAIDS Global AIDS Response Progress Reporting 2015 provided guidelines and updates on global HIV/AIDS response efforts. (Accessed October 31, 2015). 12. WHO issued guidance on couples HIV testing and counseling, including antiretroviral therapy for treatment and prevention in serodiscordant couples, emphasizing a public health approach. (Accessed September 23, 2015). 13. WHO consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection were developed to inform local implementation strategies based on epidemiology and individual risk assessments. 14. A systematic review and meta-analysis of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) trials containing tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) demonstrated its effectiveness in reducing HIV acquisition risk. Adherence was identified as a significant factor influencing efficacy. 15. HIV incidence thresholds for cost-saving implementation of PrEP vary depending on the relative costs of PrEP versus HIV treatment and its anticipated effectiveness. Offering PrEP in high-incidence settings is expected to be cost-saving in many scenarios. 16. Across all trials, PrEP was provided alongside a package of HIV prevention interventions, including regular HIV testing, counseling, condom provision, STI screening and treatment, adherence counseling, and other population-specific options. 17. Safety data from randomized controlled trials showed no significant differences in adverse event rates between PrEP and placebo groups. Subclinical declines in renal function and bone mineral density were observed but did not result in clinical events or progression over time. 18. Mathematical models predict that HIV drug resistance resulting from antiretroviral therapy (ART) far exceeds that from PrEP. Active surveillance during PrEP scale-up may be warranted to monitor resistance trends. 19. No evidence suggests that PrEP leads to risk compensation in sexual practices, such as reduced condom use or increased sexual partners. PrEP does not appear to affect hormonal contraception effectiveness, though more data are needed on interactions with hormone therapy in transgender populations.
